action.description: Action object MUST contain a field `submission`, and MAY contain arbitrary additional information.

presetHands.description: Repeated poker only. List of per-hand chance action sequences to use instead of random chance.

runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The current board has only two pieces placed, both in column 3: my x at the bottom (row 5) and the opponent's o directly above it (row 4). No lines of 3 or more exist for either player, so there are no immediate threats to block or exploit.  

Playing in column 3 now would drop my x at row 3, creating a vertical stack of x-o-x (from the bottom). The opponent can then respond in the same column to disrupt any attempt to complete 4 consecutive x pieces vertically in the upper half of the column. This leaves my pieces separated and cedes control of the center column.  

Instead, the optimal strategy is to drop adjacent to my existing x at row 5, column 3. This creates an immediate horizontal pair at the bottom row while opening strong diagonal and vertical building options in a new column. Columns 2 and 4 are symmetric and equivalent here, but column 2 starts the build on the left side without any downside. This follows standard Connect 4 opening principles for controlling the center while creating multiple future threats that the opponent cannot block simultaneously.  

No other columns (e.g., 0, 1, 5, or 6) are as strong, as they are too far from the center and my existing piece.  

Final Answer: 2

action.thoughts:
The current board has very few pieces placed (only 3 total), so this remains an early-game position with no immediate threats, forced blocks, or 3-in-a-row setups for either player. No columns are full, so all 7 moves are legal. Player x has a modest base of two adjacent pieces along the bottom row (columns 2 and 3). My existing piece (in column 3, row 4) already sits directly atop x's piece in that column.

The key evaluation is how to best extend my position for future vertical, horizontal, or diagonal lines while controlling the center (column 3 is the most strategically valuable column on a 7-wide board, as it participates in the maximum number of possible winning lines). 

- Playing in column 2 would create two horizontally adjacent pieces for me at row 4 (columns 2-3). However, this line is difficult to extend, as the adjacent columns (1 and 4) are still empty at the bottom; any future drop there would fall to row 5 rather than row 4.
- Playing in column 4 would create a diagonal connection to my existing piece but leaves the pieces disconnected from a direct vertical or horizontal line and does not maximize center control.
- Playing in column 3 drops my piece at row 3 (directly atop my existing piece). This creates two vertically connected pieces in the center column, which is far easier to extend upward (no dependency on filling lower rows in neighboring columns). It also seizes more central space for diagonals and puts pressure on x's bottom-row structure. This is strictly superior to the alternatives.

No other column (0, 1, 5, or 6) competes, as they are too far from the center and create no connections to my existing piece. This move aligns with optimal Connect 4 principles (center control and building extensible lines).

Final Answer: 3

action.thoughts:
The current board has x pieces at the bottom of columns 2 and 3, plus two o pieces stacked in column 3 (rows 1 and 2). No player has three-in-a-row yet, and the o player cannot possibly win on their next turn (they would need to reach four pieces in a line with a single drop, which is impossible from their current position).

Placing an x in column 4 drops it to row 0, creating three consecutive x pieces along the bottom row (columns 2-3-4). This position is open on both ends (columns 1 and 5). On my subsequent turn, I can always extend to four-in-a-row by dropping in the unblocked end:
- If o blocks column 1, I drop in column 5 (x in columns 2-5).
- If o blocks column 5, I drop in column 1 (x in columns 1-4).
- If o blocks neither, I can choose either.

This forces a win on my next turn regardless of o's response. (O cannot win or even create a comparable threat in the interim, as they would have only three pieces total after their move.)

Placing in column 1 creates an equivalent forcing triple (columns 1-3), but column 4 is preferable as it centers the triple more (spanning columns 2-4). All other columns are inferior: they either fail to create any three-in-a-row threat (e.g., stacking on column 2 or 3) or create a weaker/non-forcing position (e.g., column 0 or 5).

Final Answer: 4
